ClockTier.description:
How much a time is worth, graded by whether it survives being copied.

The ordering principle is copy-robustness, not accuracy. Tiers one to three travel with the
bytes. Tiers four and five describe this copy on this disk. A filesystem clock can be exact to
the nanosecond and still be a fact about when somebody moved a folder. An instrument's
acquisition time can be coarse and still be the answer to when the measurement happened.

So the ladder is principled and not arbitrary. It produces the scope boundary as a
consequence and not as a rule: prefer copy-robust clocks and the engine stops caring how files
moved.

Every rung has a source. The ND2, LIF and LI-FLIM readers fill tier one, from vendors' own
formats that the engine claims by name. The format extractors that read a document's own
metadata fill tier two. The census supplies tiers three, four and five.
ClockTier.title: ClockTier

LocatorStep.description:
One step into the interior of a file.

A locator step says how to get from a container to something inside it. A
chain of them addresses a stream at any depth: the third sheet of a workbook
inside a zip archive is two steps.
LocatorStep.title: LocatorStep

MovedBy.description:
How a walk knew a file at a new path is a file an earlier census held elsewhere (1.22).

A move is an observation about the filesystem between two censuses. It derives from both, so
the Index can reproduce it. It is never a person's decision and never a claim. The values run
from the strongest evidence to the weakest. A walk reads no content, so at walk time a match
is usually by name, size and time. The next dive that reaches the file computes a digest, and
an equal digest confirms the move.
MovedBy.title: MovedBy

ResolutionStatus.description:
Whether a question about an entity has been settled, and if not, why not.

Three of these four are absence states, and they mean different things. A
coverage figure computed over their union is not a coverage figure. It is
the conflation that this vocabulary exists to prevent.
ResolutionStatus.title: ResolutionStatus

ScanOutcome.description:
What the last run actually did with an entry.

Read by the reuse decision, which must know not only whether the file
changed but whether the previous record *delivers what today's policy asks
for*. A metadata-only record cannot satisfy a run with extraction enabled,
and an error or a deferral is never reusable. Failure is never cached, so a scan interrupted by
a stalled filesystem retries exactly the files that failed instead of serving their failures
forever.
ScanOutcome.title: ScanOutcome

SymlinkState.description:
Whether a symlink's target is there, which is not the same as whether the link is.

The engine resolves a link and never traverses it. Stating that a target exists costs one
``stat``. Walking into it turns the containment forest into a graph and can turn a scan into
an infinite one, which is why :attr:`ScanSettings.follow_symlinks` is frozen shut.

The engine keeps these states apart for a link as it does everywhere. A link whose target is
gone and a link the engine could not ask about are different states, and both differ from a
link that resolves. A stub standing in for a file that exists elsewhere is somebody's data. A
stub standing for nothing is not, and only the first is worth a person's attention.
SymlinkState.title: SymlinkState

TimeSource.description:
Where a recorded time came from. Every clock carries one.

The source is kept explicitly because a time whose provenance is unrecorded cannot be reasoned
about, and the filesystem's own clocks are the least trustworthy it offers. Creation time does
not exist on every filesystem. ``st_ctime`` means metadata change on POSIX and creation on
Windows. Copying a file usually resets both.

The content sources are split instead of gathered under one ``embedded`` value, because an
instrument's acquisition time and a word processor's "created" field are not the same kind of
fact and :class:`ClockTier` grades them differently. One value covering both would make the
tier unrecoverable from the source, which is what the pair exists to prevent.
TimeSource.title: TimeSource

description:
One thing in the data pool, filesystem object or promoted derived stream.

Every platform-dependent field is nullable. Inode, device, mode, ownership
and allocated size do not exist everywhere and are not comparable across filesystems. A schema
that requires them is a schema that lies on some machine.

Access time is deliberately absent from this record's fingerprint inputs. The
engine reads files, and a fingerprint that includes access time would record
the engine's own reading as a change to the file.
title: Entry
